---
title: "Practice: explain a substitution pathway"
---

Allow 75–90 minutes. Draw bonds, lone pairs and charges explicitly at the reacting
centre. Your explanation should connect structure, geometry and conditions.
A product formula alone is not a mechanism.

## 1. Classify the correct carbon

Draw CH₃Br, CH₃CH₂Br, CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ and (CH₃)₃CBr. Circle the carbon attached
to bromine and count how many carbon atoms are directly attached to it.
Which are methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary? Which has no neighbouring
carbon bearing a potential β-hydrogen?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The classification concerns the carbon attached to Br. A long chain can still
have a primary reaction centre if Br is at an end.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
CH₃Br is methyl (zero carbon neighbours); CH₃CH₂Br is primary (one);
CH₃CH(Br)CH₃ is secondary (two); (CH₃)₃CBr is tertiary (three). Methyl bromide
has no β-carbon. This matters for both steric approach in substitution and
the possibility of β-elimination. Carbon count alone does not settle the
outcome; the nucleophile/base, leaving group, solvent and temperature matter.
:::

## 2. Draw the methyl SN2 example

Use OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻. Show the hydroxide lone pair, the leaving-group
bond pair and the products. Draw the approach opposite Br. Is there a
carbocation intermediate? If the simple rate law is `rate = k[CH₃Br][OH⁻]`,
what happens to the initial rate when both initial concentrations double at
fixed temperature and solvent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The donor pair forms C–O as the C–Br pair returns to Br. The changes are
concerted, with no carbocation intermediate. Net charge is −1 throughout.
Doubling both concentrations gives four times the initial rate in the
supplied model, because `(2[CH₃Br]) × (2[OH⁻]) = 4[CH₃Br][OH⁻]`. This is a
kinetic prediction, not an equilibrium or isolated-yield prediction.
:::

## 3. Inversion versus a change in the letter

Build a tetrahedral carbon model with four different groups: Br, H, CH₃ and
CH₂CH₃. Place it so you can look along the C–Br bond. Replace Br by OH through
backside attack while preserving the identities of the three retained groups.
Draw before and after using wedge/dash bonds. Assign priorities independently
to each drawing and then give the R/S labels.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The tetrahedral arrangement inverts at the reacting carbon. For this particular
2-bromobutane → butan-2-ol comparison, Br and OH are each highest priority in
their respective structures; ethyl ranks above methyl and H is lowest. Thus
an S starting configuration gives R in the product, or vice versa. The
general mechanistic rule is geometric inversion. In other replacements,
priorities may change, so do not infer a new letter without checking them.
:::

## 4. Work through an SN1 model in water

For a tertiary alkyl bromide `(CH₃)₃CBr`, draw these **separate** stages:
ionisation; attack by water; removal of a proton by another water molecule.
Show charges after every stage. Explain why the first stage is more plausible
for this substrate than for CH₃Br. Name one possible product of a competing
pathway starting from the same carbocation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Water oxygen starts with two bonds. After it bonds to carbon but before it
loses a proton, count its bonds again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The C–Br pair moves to Br, giving `(CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻`. A water lone pair attacks
the carbocation, giving `(CH₃)₃COH₂⁺`. Another water removes H⁺ to give
`(CH₃)₃COH + H₃O⁺`. Bromide remains a spectator after ionisation. The tertiary
carbocation is stabilised by its carbon substituents relative to a methyl
carbocation. Loss of β-H from the carbocation can instead yield
2-methylpropene through E1. Neither the substrate name nor water alone tells
you the precise product ratio.
:::

## 5. Why is a neutral alcohol not automatically a good substrate?

A proposed step shows OH⁻ leaving directly from an ordinary neutral alcohol
to form a carbocation. Identify the problem. Draw an acid–base activation step
that could make water the departing group, and explain why the resulting
substitution/elimination outcome still requires substrate and conditions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Hydroxide is a poor leaving group in the selected conditions. Protonating
the alcohol oxygen gives an oxonium species that can lose neutral water.
This activation does not make every alcohol react by SN1: carbocation
stability, availability of nucleophiles/bases and other conditions determine
whether a concerted, stepwise or competing elimination route is plausible.
:::

## 6. Explain a substrate-and-condition choice

Compare methyl bromide with a strong nucleophile to a tertiary bromide in a
polar aqueous medium. Write a short justified pathway proposal for each.
Include one limitation of your proposal; for example, a competing process or
information needed before predicting an experimental product proportion.

## Leave with

Two complete mechanisms, an inversion drawing and an explanation linking each
pathway to its reacting centre and medium. Consult the
[reading guide](../reference/reading.qmd) for selected Solomons chapter 6 support.
